'''Alan Reginald Bishop''' is an internationally recognized British/American [[physicist]] and academic, specializing in [[condensed matter theory]], [[statistical physics]], and [[Nonlinear system|nonlinear]] physics. He retired as Principal Associate Director - Science, Technology, and Engineering at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] in 2018.

He has made major contributions in the areas of [[soliton]]s, [[quantum complexity theory|quantum complexity]], structural and magnetic transitions, [[quasiparticle|collective excitations]] in low-dimensional organic and inorganic materials and complex electronic materials with strong spin-charge-lattice coupling.  Among his numerous seminal contributions, the Peyrard-Bishop model<ref>{{cite journal|title=A nonlinear dynamic model of DNA with a sequence-dependent stacking term|url= |journal=Nucleic Acids Research|year=2009|doi=10.1093/nar/gkp016|last1=Alexandrov|first1=B. S.|last2=Gelev|first2=V.|last3=Monisova|first3=Y.|last4=Alexandrov|first4=L. B.|last5=Bishop|first5=A. R.|last6=Rasmussen|first6=K. O.|last7=Usheva|first7=A.|volume=37|issue=7|pages=2405–2410|pmid=19264801|pmc=2673413}}</ref> of DNA denaturation is well known. He is a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (1983), [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation|Humboldt Foundation]] Senior Fellow (2000), Fellow of [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] (2004), Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (2006), and Fellow of [[Institute of Physics]] (UK, 2011).  He has edited about 20 books and journal issues. He has served as a consultant with [[IBM Research]] Lab, Zurich, Max-Planck Institute, Stuttgart, International Centre for Theoretical Physics, Trieste among many others. He has published more than 750 papers with over 32,000 citations and an [[h-index]] of 82 (Google Scholar).{{citation needed|date=June 2021}}

Born in [[Staffordshire]], [[England]], he was educated at the [[University of East Anglia]] and [[Trinity College, Cambridge]] (PhD, 1973).<ref>{{cite web|title=Principal Associate Director - Science, Technology, and Engineering|url=http://www.lanl.gov/about/leadership-governance/science-technology-engineering.php|website=[[Los Alamos National Laboratory]]|access-date=19 September 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=The Cambridge University List of Members Up to 31 December 1988}}</ref> He obtained his Ph.D. with (future, 1977) Nobel Laureates Sir [[Neville Mott]] and [[Philip W. Anderson]]. After positions as a junior research fellow at [[Oxford University]] (with Sir [[Roger Elliott (physicist)|Roger Elliott]]), research associate at [[Cornell University]] (with future, 1989, [[American Physical Society|APS]] president [[James A. Krumhansl|Jim Krumhansl]]) and a lecturer at [[University of London]], he arrived at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] as a staff scientist in 1979. In 1980 he co-founded the Center for Nonlinear Studies (CNLS)<ref>{{cite web|title=Center for Nonlinear Studies|url=https://cnls.lanl.gov/External/|website=CNLS}}</ref> at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]] and served as its Acting/Deputy Chairman.  During 1984 – 1999 he was the group leader of the Condensed Matter and Statistical Physics Group, then during 1999 – 2006 as Division Leader of the Theoretical Division.  From 2006 – 2011 he served as the associate director for theory, simulation and computing and finally became the principal associate director for science, technology and engineering (during 2011- 2018). Currently he is a senior lab fellow and a guest scientist. He was awarded the [[Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award]] in 1993.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award|url=http://science.energy.gov/lawrence/award-laureates/1990s/bishop/|website=[[United States Department of Energy]]|access-date=19 September 2016}}</ref> In 2024, he was awarded the Los Alamos Medal, the laboratory's highest honor.<ref>{{Cite web |last=LANL |title=Alan Bishop and Brad Meyer win the Los Alamos Medal {{!}} LANL |url=https://www.lanl.gov/media/news/0924-la-medal |access-date=2025-07-23 |website=Los Alamos National Laboratory |language=en}}</ref> He has also served on a dozen advisory boards, including at the Mind Institute, Albuquerque. He is on the committee of the [[Stefanos Pnevmatikos International Award]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.physics.uoc.gr/Pnevmatikos/index1.html |title= Selection Committee |author=<!--Not stated--> |date= |website= Stefanos Pnevmatikos International Award |publisher= University of Crete |access-date= 29 May 2018 |quote=}}</ref>
